blocks.x: Now, since this last oral history was done for the Smithsonian, you have met and married Fatu. Talk about that whole evolution and how you met Fatu, and the story of your getting married.
Well, I’ll make it short. I won’t spend too much time talking about marriage. (Laughs)
Well, I mean the whole marriage thing that has a spiritual aspect to it, too.

Well, what happened was, I met my wife, Fatoumata Mbengue. She’s a Lebo woman, Wulluf, from Senegal. She has a beautiful African shop in Paris. We met because some of the Gnawans invited her to my concert in Paris, with Gnawa. So she saw me before I saw her. I passed her shop many times and never went in for some reason, but I realized when I went in that that was it; I’d never come out again. (Laughs) I finally

went into the shop after two or three trips from New York back to Paris. She saw me, I never saw her. What happened was, because I was invited because a photographer named Ariane Smolderen, she’s from Belgium; we made trips to Morocco to photograph a history of the Gnawa people. We traveled Fez, to Marrakech, to Telouet, to Agadir, we went down the Sahara just photographing Gnawa families, because there are different parts of Morocco. She was close to a woman in Paris who was from Belgium. She owned a gallery, and they were having a conference on Sufi music in Gwana, in Egypt. Gwana is near Karnak, Egypt.
